author: Shirley Killen
title: Building the socialist movement in regional Victoria
content:
Victorians from Mildura to Mallacoota will have the chance to vote socialist for the first time in generations at this month’s state election. In a campaign that’s been full of milestones for the Victorian Socialists, one of the biggest is that the party is standing candidates in all 88 lower house seats for the first time. 

Networks of socialist activists have sprung up across the state with the goal of getting these candidates elected, putting on meetings, organising local rallies, door knocking and letterboxing. In some places, like Bendigo and Ballarat, local branches already existed, while in others, coordinators are starting from scratch.

David Suter is one of the local coordinators starting from scratch. He describes turning up to a polling booth after moving to Garfield, in eastern Victoria and part of the electorate of Narracan, looking at his options and thinking “this is bullshit”. The dearth of organised radical politics in regional areas could easily make a person feel disheartened. But David was encouraged by the result the Victorian Socialists achieved in last year’s federal election, so he signed up to attend the party’s state conference later that year. He left with a list of phone numbers and a plan to activate socialists in his region, and established a crew of seven who began sketching out a state election campaign. Now, the party has candidates contesting all eleven lower house seats, and the beginnings of local branches in Narracan, Shepparton, Bairnsdale and the Mornington Peninsula—to name just a few. 

These are “baby steps”, according to David. It’s a big task to rebuild (or just build, sometimes) a socialist tradition in regional Victoria. But the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign so far has proved it is not impossible, and that with a common goal and some organisational infrastructure, socialists who previously felt isolated in the regions can make a difference.

Renee Nayef, the Victorian Socialists candidate for Mildura in Victoria’s north-west, described a “meet the candidate” event she put on recently. Two men drove into Mildura separately from a nearby town of 97 people, both assuming they were the only socialists for kilometres. They met for the first time at Renee’s event. Without the scaffolding of a statewide socialist campaign, they might have gone on for years not knowing there was another radical a couple of streets over. 

Sometimes these connections are made in unorthodox ways. For socialist campaigners in metropolitan Melbourne, the movement is built by knocking on other people’s doors and starting up conversations about socialism. Socialists in the regions report the opposite experience—locals are instead knocking on 

their 

doors because they’ve seen a yard sign and are thrilled to know there’s another socialist in town. 

In some parts of the state, the campaign is reviving largely forgotten radical traditions. Bass candidate for Victorian Socialists Chris Jobe had to correct the record when the local paper announced his candidacy with the headline “Red flag planted in Bass for the first time”. In fact, the seat of Bass takes in the old mining town Wonthaggi, known for much of the twentieth century as “Red Wonthaggi” because of the militancy of the local communist-led miners’ union. A more accurate headline would have been “Red flag planted in Bass 

again

”. 

The picture in regional Victoria today is clearly very different from the days when the Wonthaggi miners fought bitter industrial battles with coal bosses and the state. With few exceptions, these seats are the preserve of the Liberals and Nationals, with One Nation now poised to make serious gains. Socialists campaigning outside Melbourne don’t sugarcoat the challenges they are facing.

But socialist politics haven’t been seriously tested outside the state’s biggest cities in decades. It’s not surprising that conservative politics dominate when there’s nothing much else on offer. 

And working-class people in rural Victoria face the same stresses as their counterparts in Melbourne. The rising cost of living, the health system stretched to breaking point, the failure of successive governments to invest in transport and education—these issues are coming up all across the state. 

For Hera Sheppard, Victorian Socialists candidate for the South-West Coast, it was growing up in Warrnambool’s public housing that made her a socialist. She witnessed the way Labor neglected its housing stock and failed to address ballooning waiting lists for housing. Later, she got a job at McDonald's, only to experience all the injustices of being a young worker, from copping junior pay rates to dodging live electrical wires at work. She’s proud of her efforts to unionise McDonald's and enter bargaining for the first time in a decade. But perhaps the greatest compliment came from the 

Portland Observer

, which ran an article about her candidacy with the headline “Sheppard vows to stand up for workers”.

Renee’s grandparents migrated to Mildura from Greece and worked picking and packing grapes in tin sheds in 40-degree heat. She says growing up in the region exposed her to the racism of Australian capitalism, the brutal dispossession and segregation endured by Aboriginal communities and the injustice of a society where those who work the hardest have to scrimp and save just to get by. She’s running to “give hope to people across Victoria that the world can be different if we fight for it”.

In Bendigo, coordinator (and local councillor) Owen Cosgriff jokes that if the outer northern and western suburbs of Melbourne are the front lines of the state election campaign, then he and his comrades are several hundred kilometres “deep in enemy territory”. But even so, he expects they’ll be staffing all four pre-poll booths in Bendigo and Castlemaine, and a sizeable number of the election day voting centres. This is a major achievement for a socialist party any day of the week—and they’ve got big plans to keep building after the election, with a new Castlemaine branch on the horizon.

“Baby steps”. That’s how David describes the work he’s helping to coordinate across eastern Victoria. But only from baby steps can bigger things ever come.

author: Sarah Garnham
title: One Nation is waging war on progress. Why won't progressives fight back?
content:
In 2018, One Nation struggled to get registered as a political party in Victoria, and progressives across the state took pride in it. Labor won the state election that year with a whopping 43 percent primary vote. Twenty years earlier, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson had been prevented from organising in Melbourne by protests, blockades and community events.

Today, the snarling menace and enemy of workers and the left that is One Nation is a major force in Victoria; it enjoys mass support, is vying for lower house seats, and setting the agenda in the state election campaign. The party and its policies have been legitimised by the capitalist press, the Liberal Party and, to a lesser extent, Labor. One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, has been invited to appear at the leaders’ debate.  

Progressive Victoria should be in uproar. This is the state of Trades Hall, Treaty and Pride. But aside from a few important exceptions—most notably high school students—the response to One Nation’s rise has been decidedly muted. Progressive NGOs and organisations have mostly stayed silent or offered tepid statements focusing on the fears of their constituents rather than forthright denunciation of One Nation and all it represents. The mood is closer to stunned awe than anger, almost as if the capacity to generate the ever-more-elusive commodity of popularity makes a party worthy of respect, however the popularity might be gained. 

Worse still, a layer of trade union organisers, Greens members and other progressives is arguing that the left must sympathise with the concerns of One Nation voters, or at least avoid antagonising them through political argument. In practice, this means sidestepping the signature issues that One Nation is pushing and building a base around. 

GetUp and Victorian Trades Hall Council (VTHC) are 

directing

 campaigners not to “play the racism card” or explicitly attack Pauline Hanson. After its costly and high-profile intervention in the Farrer by-election, GetUp concluded that criticising Hanson, her wealthy backer Gina Rinehart, celebrity defector Barnaby Joyce or the party’s links to Trump is not electorally expedient. Campaigners should instead seek to establish common ground with potential One Nation voters based on economic grievances. 

Senior VTHC researcher Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett 

argues

 to ignore the politics: “Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying”. The beat, he says, is dissatisfaction with the status quo, so supporters should be helped to “tease out” what that looks like and how it makes them feel. 

Federal Greens leader David Shoebridge 

says

 he has “understood the anger” driving One Nation support. Former Queensland Greens MP Max Chandler-Mathers 

goes further

, arguing that One Nation voters, especially the workers among them, are expressing legitimate protest against the system. He says they are driven by an “almost political nihilism”, and a desire to “blow it up” that makes them open to left-wing arguments and solutions. 

The same basic approach is being taken by more establishment political forces. Teal consultant Sue Barret gives the 

same advice

in four steps: validate the feeling, not the target; ask a genuine question and then be quiet; acknowledge the ground you share; offer a different path, not a different diagnosis.

Labor’s federal treasurer likewise 

warns

 progressives not to “scold” One Nation supporters, and to approach them “from a place of genuine respect and understanding”. The same advice is given by the media, from the establishment right through to liberal outlets. And all of this helps to reinforce One Nation’s 

spin

 about itself: that it is the party of “everyday Australians” who are “sick and tired of being ignored”. 

This appeasement goes further than merely tempering criticisms of One Nation for fear of alienating the party’s voters; it leads to actively opposing efforts to build resistance. 

The Labor-controlled National Union of Students, for example, pulled out of supporting the second student walkout against One Nation, and attacked office bearers for promoting it. Some Greens MPs have endorsed and spoken at the rallies, but others refused to speak on the grounds that it is not strategic and would alienate bigots. When a socialist promoted an anti-One Nation rally in a union activist online forum, the Victorian secretary of the CPSU and long-time leftist Jiselle Hanna replied that it is “more powerful to understand why so many of the working class are being persuaded by One Nation, than dismissing them all as a bunch of racists”. She then removed unionists who backed the protest from the forum.

What is going on?

For some, the lack of interest in denouncing or confronting far-right supporters today comes from a sense of defeatism: One Nation is connecting with the moment better than our side of politics, so we have no credibility to challenge it. Unfortunately, this only leads to further normalisation of the right and the further weakening of our side. 

For others, it may be that they see protest and other forms of resistance aimed at polarising sentiment as an outdated method. Yet history is full of successful movements against the far right. In the 1990s, mass and sustained demonstrations helped push One Nation back to the margins. Last month in Serbia, a two-year, student-led protest movement ended the rule of a right-wing nationalist government. Even if the far right can’t be defeated immediately, efforts towards building mass resistance have more to recommend them than cowering passivity.

But by far the most pervasive argument made by progressives is that One Nation voters are confused victims of the system and therefore potentially open to influence. The stereotype of the everyday person fed up with official politics, the major parties and motivated primarily by their bread-and-butter concerns, is the common-sense explanation of the rise of the “populist” right in Australia as well as many other places. 

Commentators across the political spectrum have their own version of it, with flourishes based on their particular political outlook. Right-wing journalist Phil Coorey

 

says

 

people are pining for an Australia before multiculturalism and “elite progressivism”. Labor-aligned Kos Samaras 

says

 they are the victims of disintegrating local community, health and public services. Chandler-Mathers

 

says

 

the hollowing-out of collective organisation has “left a febrile and unstable political democracy because now the vast majority of people are completely disconnected from either major party”, with housing and financial stress as the spark.

But as French anti-fascist writer Andrew Hussey has 

noted

, “populism” is a dubious label. It is applied to parties of the right in a way that reflects “the elitist prejudice that the people are ignorant and irrational, impulsive and incoherent, easily manipulated and prone to authoritarian excess and frenzies of xenophobia”. Political disengagement is high, and incoherence is its corollary, but the idea that One Nation voters cannot meaningfully be associated with the party’s actual politics is misorienting.

It is these politics that matter the most. The reasons why people might vote for One Nation do not determine what it stands for. And there is little ambiguity on this score: a new White Australia, mass deportations, attacks on workers’ rights, more freedom for business, fewer environmental protections and more power for the state to lock people up and repress dissent.

Like its counterparts worldwide, its program is a reaction to every progressive advance since the last major wave of struggle in the 1960s and ’70s, dressed up as no-nonsense common sense. It defines itself against pro-Palestine sentiment, migrant and refugee rights, strong unions, women’s rights, trans inclusion, net zero and public health measures. It opposes these not because they are aspects of a neoliberal status quo, but because they represent the agenda of the left and the working-class movement. 

One Nation sees the major parties as having bowed to these “woke” demands and is open about its intention to reverse them. Whatever individual voters feel, this is the goal of the party and the corporate donors that bankroll it. This is what distinguishes it from all the other parties. And it’s why One Nation has made the greatest gains when political developments have favoured this reactionary agenda. Indeed, the party’s key breakthrough from the margins to the mainstream came following the Bondi massacre, when anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, ultra-nationalist sentiment was at a righteous high.

A preoccupation with sugar-coating the support base of One Nation, and the assumption underlying it that One Nation supporters are uniquely disconnected from the formal politics of the party for some unexplained reason, has the effect of downplaying the importance of One Nation’s formal politics and the threat they pose. The beneficiaries of this emphasis are those, like the Labor Party, wanting to adopt elements of One Nation’s policies, whether because they have no alternative agenda to argue convincingly for, they want to chase the right-wing vote or because they recognise that many in the capitalist class approve of those policies, and that’s what matters to them. 

These forces will do anything to avoid admitting that a significant section of the population has been won over to supporting a fascist-adjacent political machine. To do so means facing up to the inherent responsibility to resist.     

So what should we do?

First, we need to acknowledge that One Nation is a reactionary blight on society. To confront it, we need to have two approaches simultaneously. The first is to build opposition to One Nation in the here and now, by being clear and firm about how reactionary the party is and by mobilising and giving confidence to those already hostile to it. The second is the longer-term project of rebuilding a strong left, tied to a powerful workers’ movement, on the scale needed to decisively set the far right back. Those arguing for pandering to One Nation supporters are working towards neither. 

Chandler-Mathers 

argues

 for a Greens program of “progressive populism”, to be presented via one-on-one conversations that don’t challenge voters’ diagnosis of the problems with the system but offer alternative policies, such as better services, welfare and wealth redistribution. He regularly cites anecdotes to endorse this approach, for instance winning a One Nation voter to the Greens by explaining their free lunches program. For him and others on the Greens’ left, this strategy is the bedrock of an ambition to electorally replace Labor. 

The unions offer a similar approach: one-on-one conversations with workers flirting with the right, focused on Hanson’s anti-worker record, with a vote for Labor as the hopeful outcome. They refuse to hold Labor responsible for attacks on the working class—even unions that have scaled back their campaigning efforts in the Victorian election still orient to it and lobby it. The VTHC 

pamphlet

 by Kaspi-Crutchett, 

Antidote: trade unionism as a vaccine against far-right politics

, argues that unions offer workers a better cultural home and identity, and that union membership correlates with voting Labor. It says a lot about the movement’s low horizons that the pamphlet makes no case for industrial struggle and power, either to win working-class demands or to build support for working-class politics.

For socialists, politics isn’t about offering a program to a passive public. It isn’t about convincing individuals to vote for what we decide is good for them. It is about winning arguments at a deeper level, to actually change people’s worldview to one of recognising working-class interests and power. And it is about building a movement that can impose that worldview on society, that can chalk up wins for workers and the oppressed, and demonstrate in practice that the left has the answers. Elections are part of that, but left electoral programs will only be truly effective as an extension of existing class power and organisation. 

If we did have a strong fighting left and union movement right now, it would be possible to make a meaningful dent in the momentum of the far right. We could have mass protests against racism, in support of migrant rights and demonstrations of solidarity between workers across racial lines. Unions could arrest the cost-of-living crisis, win higher wages for particular groups of workers and force broader social gains like price controls, interest payment freezes and more funding for services. We could extend the Palestine movement to force the government to break ties with Israel and build a powerful anti-war movement against AUKUS and the US alliance. We could stop the construction of AI data centres, force the government to build public housing and put the environment before the profits of fossil fuel companies. We could put black bans on projects connected to Rinehart, Musk or any far-right figures here or globally, and organise hospitality staff and others to ensure Hanson and her cronies can’t meet in peace anywhere, as happened in the movement against the apartheid South African Springbok tour.

This is the kind of power and momentum the left needs to strive to build. Such a movement would then open the way to arguing with reactionary layers and with workers who hold backward ideas, both by having a bigger platform from which to attack their politics and through our ability to impose ours. A serious working-class force could also pose real solutions to most grievances—not as a defensive offering in exchange for a vote, but as an alternative to dog-eat-dog capitalism. In this context, sections of the middle class, such as small business owners, can be won to a program that disciplines the big capitalists and provides welfare for all.

This also raises the question of power. If the collective organisation of workers, in bodies like workplace and strike committees, can win gains, why not maintain them as day-to-day governing bodies rather than just defensive organisations? This starts to become a challenge to the power of the capitalist class in its entirety and raises the possibility of a different type of society based on direct democratic control of society’s wealth: socialism.

We are a long way from such a movement. The long-term degeneration of the unions and the left means we lack the forces, influence and capacity to initiate the struggle that is needed, and the right far outnumbers us. It has international and domestic conditions in its favour and will remain a serious force for the medium term, whatever One Nation’s exact electoral results. History offers no blueprint for stopping the far right’s momentum, though successful anti-fascist movements contain many lessons. But we have to keep in our sights the scale of the movement and organised force needed to push it back.

We have to start somewhere. That means building among people who are horrified by One Nation and can recognise it for what it is, and drawing them together to act, organising protests and resistance, and by putting our political opposition to the far right front and centre. Our dealings with the far right should be about confronting and denouncing its politics, not excusing it through sympathy with its supporters, or nodding along when they scapegoat their migrant neighbours. 

The far right have in part been successful because they know their enemy and fight it ruthlessly. They do not focus on how misunderstood and decent left-wing people are. They detest us and everything we stand for, and use that hatred to build. We need to do the same.

Beyond organising opposition to the far right, we need to build the power and institutions of our side generally. The organised socialist movement is the force that can draw together the immediate and long-term tasks we face: that can offer staunch and principled opposition to the far right today, and that can work towards the kind of power and struggle necessary to defeat it and the entire system that breeds it.

author: Nick Everett
title: Remembering the Santa Cruz massacre
content:
Thirty-five years ago, Indonesian elite Kopassus troops opened fire on a peaceful procession in Dili, the capital of then Indonesian-occupied East Timor (today known as Timor Leste), killing hundreds. The Indonesian generals responsible have never faced justice, protected by the Western governments who armed them and abetted their crimes. 

The procession, on the morning of 12 November 1991, followed a memorial mass at Motael Church for Sebastião Gomes Rangel, a young Timorese man killed by Indonesian security forces two weeks earlier. As the procession of 3,000 mourners made its way to Santa Cruz cemetery, pro-independence banners and flags were unfurled. Minutes after the crowd arrived at the cemetery, troops opened fire without warning.

Shooting continued as people tried to scale the cemetery’s high walls. Some were shot in the back while running away. Others while seeking shelter behind tombstones or in the cemetery’s chapel. More were stabbed and shot as they lay on the ground in pools of blood. According to survivor testimonies, dozens more were executed or disappeared after being taken to the Wira Husada Military Hospital. 

At least 271 East Timorese were killed that day, and an equal number disappeared, believed dead, according to the East Timor Action Network.

Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans was quick to defend Indonesia’s military, which had invaded East Timor in December 1975 and maintained a brutal occupation of the former Portuguese colony. A month after the massacre, Evans 

told

 parliament that while the incident was “‘deplorable”, it “was not ... a calculated or deliberate act of the [Indonesian] government as such”. Rather, it was “the product of aberrant behaviour by a subgroup within the country”. 

Two years earlier, Evans had joined his Indonesian counterpart, Ali Alatas, to toast the signing of the Timor Gap Treaty in a plane above the Timor Sea. With a glass of champagne in his hand, Evans declared: “This is a uniquely historical moment that is truly, uniquely historical”.

The treaty, several years in the making, carved up the rich oil and gas resources beneath the Timor Sea and opened the way for their exploitation by Australian resource companies. 

The Santa Cruz massacre was not unique. Many had preceded it, including the Kraras massacres, in the southern municipality of Viqueque in 1983. Prabowo Subianto, a rising star in the army and the son-in-law of Indonesian dictator, General Suharto, commanded the Kopassus special forces unit responsible. 

The Kraras massacres have been 

compared

 with the US army’s massacre of Vietnamese civilians in the village of Mai Lai in 1968. Much like the strategy pursued by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon, such attacks sought to isolate combatants via major military operations that killed and displaced large numbers of civilians.

In 2005, East Timor’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (CAVR) 

concluded

 that Indonesia’s 24-year-long occupation resulted in between 102,800 and 183,000 conflict-related deaths, alongside widespread systematic torture, unlawful killings, enforced disappearances, forced displacement, and sexual violence. Many human rights organisations, including 

Genocide Watch

, argue that Indonesia committed a genocide in East Timor.

What made the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre different from those that preceded it was that it was caught on 

film

. When British cameraman Max Stahl’s footage was subsequently broadcast, it shone a light on Indonesia’s crimes and revived a global solidarity movement.

In Australia in the 1990s, socialists led a campaign group called Action in Solidarity with Indonesia and East Timor (ASIET), which coordinated demonstrations in conjunction with other East Timor solidarity groups across the country to commemorate the Santa Cruz massacre on 12 November each year.

We argued that the overthrow of Indonesia’s military dictatorship would open the road to Timorese independence, and that we therefore needed to support not only the resistance to the occupation, but also the growing student and worker movements in Indonesia that were calling for an end to Suharto’s military rule. We demanded that our own government break military ties with Indonesia.

Military and diplomatic ties between the two countries were extensive and growing, and by 1996 included a military pact. At the time, Australia was training Kopassus forces at the Kokoda Barracks on the Gold Coast. The Keating government also shamefully (and hypocritically) denied protection visas to East Timorese asylum seekers on the grounds that they were entitled to Portuguese citizenship.

The close Canberra-Jakarta relationship was staunchly defended in the Australian media. Writing in the 

Sydney Morning Herald

 on 9 December 1994, right-wing columnist Padraic (Paddy) McGuiness declared that “the alleged ‘genocide’ of the East Timorese population is a myth, assiduously cultivated by the propagandists and their dupes”.

These arguments would be familiar to anyone who has been involved in opposing Israel’s Gaza genocide.

In May 1998, Suharto was overthrown amidst a deep financial crisis. His successor, B.J. Habibi, was now forced to make concessions to the insurgent, student-led pro-democracy movement. General Prabowo stood accused of responsibility for the kidnapping and torturing pro-democracy Indonesian activists in Jakarta in the preceding months. Thirteen were forcibly disappeared, never to be seen again. 

Having now lost his protection, Prabowo was thrown out of the army. Habibi also reluctantly agreed to grant East Timorese a referendum on their future. In August 1999, they voted overwhelmingly for independence, despite a violent campaign of intimidation by the Indonesian military, including a series of brutal massacres. 

Under growing international pressure, Indonesia was forced to abandon its military occupation and hand control of the territory to a UN occupation force, known as UNTAET. In May 2002, Timor Leste finally gained its formal independence.

While Suharto’s overthrow led to a period of 

reformasi

—democratic elections took place for the first time in 30 years—today, the military is back in business in Jakarta. Prabowo has not only escaped justice. He is now Indonesia’s president. 

And in Timor Leste, a nation desperate for foreign investment, former resistance leaders Xanana Gusmao and José Ramos Horta, now prime minister and president, routinely roll out the red carpet for Indonesian dignitaries, including former generals.

The Santa Cruz massacre is a reminder that justice is at best momentary and fleeting in a world carved up into spheres of interest between competing imperial powers. 

In 1961, observing the process of decolonisation in Africa, Franz Fanon wrote in the 

Wretched of the Earth

: “The apotheosis of independence is transformed into the curse of independence, and the colonial power through its immense resources of coercion condemns the young nation to regression”.

In other words, without dismantling the system of oppression that binds us all, independence means little more than a flag and an anthem. 

Nick is the former Brisbane Coordinator for Action in Solidarity with Indonesia and East Timor

author: Editors
title: Historic Victorian election an opportunity to rebuild socialist organisation
content:
The Victorian election will be a significant moment in Australian politics. 

The ALP, which has ruled the state for most of the last three decades, looks set to take a significant hit to its primary vote. A DemosAU poll has Labor’s primary vote at 18 percent, just one point ahead of the Greens. Resolve’s reporting had them at 22 percent, which is nevertheless a record low and well down on the 37 percent primary vote they received in the 2022 state election.

Meanwhile, far-right One Nation has entered the political field as a serious challenger to the major parties, if polling is accurate. The once-pariah party is now firmly part of the mainstream, as are its fascist-adjacent politics. And the Liberals, who last election were declared too “weak and divided” and facing too serious an “identity crisis” to govern by the 

Age

, now enjoy the backing of almost all the corporate media. 

The much more dispersed nature of the vote makes the outcome difficult to predict. 

Labor’s leaders have essentially given up on winning; every MP is now in a desperate fight to save their own seat and career. The union movement has largely abandoned the field, with a number belatedly refusing to campaign for Labor.

Even the premier is looking likely to lose his seat. Good riddance.

Carroll’s strategy of shifting the party hard to the right by attacking the CFMEU and boosting the spectre of youth crime is backfiring, alienating what little support the ALP had left. His short time in office will be quickly forgotten, but his legacy—of demoralising working-class Labor voters and legitimising the various attacks the incoming Liberal government has planned—will remain. 

In his place will step Jess Wilson as the head of a resurgent Liberal Party. Her plan is there for all to see. Savage cuts to the public service. A ban on protests without police permission. Censorship of the pro-Palestine movement. Ripping up the Treaty.

Wilson has promised to recall parliament before Christmas, not to address housing affordability or the crisis in our hospitals, but to introduce harsher bail laws and put more kids in jail. All of this she’s hoping to do in a Trump-style 100-day blitz, during which she will serve as both premier and treasurer.

Wilson has been sold to the public as a moderate, a relatable millennial and a fresh face. The capitalist press, including the

 Age 

and the 

Guardian

,

 

have done their bit to popularise this image.

Her history suggests something quite different. She has been a Liberal apparatchik since her university days at Monash, after which she worked at disgraced consultancy firm KPMG, before jumping ship to be a policy executive at the Business Council of Australia.

Her Institute of Public Affairs-aligned husband stood down as a Liberal candidate in 2014 after it was revealed he referred to gay men as “faggots”. They remain happily married.

The truth is that Wilson is a trained class warrior for the billionaires and the bosses. Aside from the culture wars and the 

UFC fight nights

, the key goal of her campaign is to balance the state’s budget and cut taxes on the corporate elite.

The blatant contradiction between these two goals can only be resolved through swingeing cuts to health care, education and other vital public services, mass sackings and the privatisation of state assets. She has already flagged her desire to do both, though the financial press are demanding that she cut much harder and deeper.

In addition to the prospect of a slash-and-burn, Kennett-style Liberal government, workers will face a One Nation party that is set to win an unprecedented vote. These far-right nutters will exercise a constant rightward pressure on the Liberals, particularly when the latter seek to pass legislation through the upper house, where One Nation may well hold the balance of power. They will also use their platform to attack the rights of workers and women while demonising migrants and other oppressed groups.

But while official politics is shifting sharply to the right, there are plenty of people looking for an alternative. Despite the tidal wave of establishment hostility directed at the Greens because of the party’s strong stance on Gaza, they look set for a meaningful increase in their primary vote.

More importantly for the radical left, the Victorian Socialists campaign has been easily the biggest yet. More than 2,000 people have participated in public meetings, door knocks, phone banks and rallies across the state.

Fielding a candidate in every seat has been an immense achievement, radically expanding the presence of socialist politics. All of this means that Victorian Socialists have a very real chance of electing a socialist to parliament for the first time in many decades. Both Anneke Demanuele, running in the Western Metropolitan district, and Omar Hassan, running in the Northern Metropolitan district, are serious contenders to be elected to the upper house. 

But while it would be great to get a socialist into parliament, one of the most important aspects of the campaign is how it has helped cohere more socialists and built the sorts of organisation we will need for the battles that are to come.

Coming out of this election campaign, Victorian Socialists will have 30 functioning branches, from the outer suburbs of Melbourne to regional cities like Geelong, Ballarat, Shepparton and Bendigo. These growing networks of working-class militants, many still very new to organising, mean we will not have to start from scratch when the next government starts attacking schools, hospitals and other services in the name of reducing the debt. 

Branches of Victorian Socialists can and should become a focal point for not only organising action but also political discussion and education. They provide a space where people can learn and compare notes about organising in their workplaces, universities or schools. They can become hubs which can attract disaffected Labor and Greens members keen to see a more radical approach to politics, as well as workers and young people engaging with the socialist left for the first time.

Throughout history, it has been socialists who have been central to building the infrastructure of working-class resistance to the system—from trade unions to explosive student and political struggles. The co-option and absorption of many of the twentieth century radicals into a rightward-moving ALP has left workers defenceless in the face of neoliberal attacks from Labor and Liberal alike.

And while it will still be some time and take some serious effort before we can lead workers in epic battles like the 1986 Victorian nurses’ strike, or organise unions as political as the NSW Builders Labourers Federation in the 1970s—let alone abolish capitalism—building a serious socialist organisation takes us an important step closer to this goal. Every person who joins can make an important contribution, and together we can better carry forward the radical traditions that have won so much of what we value today. 

The task of building a mass socialist party is more pressing than ever. There is no compromise possible with a ruling class that allows climate breakdown and social decay, unleashes fascist mobs and perpetual wars, backs trillionaires and their data centres, and forces us into an endless grind to pay the bills.

Only socialism offers answers radical enough to meet the scale of these crises, to smash the out of touch elites who are driving so many to despair about the future. Only socialism offers the vision of a better world democratically run by the mass of working-class people, where the immense resources of society are used to improve the lives of the mass of humanity.

All across Europe we have seen important stirrings of revolt. In France, for week after week, high school student have sustained school blockades and occupations in defiance of brutal police repression and have drawn in behind them university students, their teachers and other workers.

The heroism and determination of these young working-class students has inspired waves of protests and strikes across the continent by workers and students fed up with the ongoing attacks on their living standards, the growing far-right threat and any hope of a decent future in twenty-first century capitalism. Now in Spain, 5 million workers have stopped work and taken to the streets in a massive general strike.

The urgent task now is to build a serious socialist fighting force in every country that can lead these inspiring struggles to victory. Here in Australia, the Victorian Socialists election campaign is one small but important step in that direction. We need everyone who aspires to see a better world of genuine human freedom to make a stand and join us.

author: Yasmine Johnson
title: Jillian Segal’s war on the left
content:
Antisemitism Special Envoy Jillian Segal’s “Plan to combat antisemitism” is nothing of the sort. Her latest report, published 30 October, is a stunning piece of Trumpist propaganda. It is riddled with conspiracy theories about malign radical-left and Islamist influence in Australian institutions. It calls for sweeping crackdowns on free speech, political activism and migration, all in the name of protecting Israel’s reputation. It is an indictment of the Labor government that commissioned it.

Labor named Segal “special envoy to combat antisemitism” knowing her record as a right-wing warrior and campaigner for Israel’s murderous wars. Her appointment was part of a multi-faceted offensive against the Palestine solidarity movement. She has consistently used this platform to shield the Israeli government from criticism and attack opponents of the war.

Segal’s new report pays little attention to the growing antisemitic far right. Since her appointment, Nazis have addressed thousands at anti-migrant marches. One Nation, a party 

riddled with Hitler fanatics

, has shot up in the polls. But far-right antisemitism is minimised because it isn’t the “primary source of concern or anxiety to members of the Jewish community”.

The real danger is “modern, progressive antisemitism”, which Segal labels “the most pervasive manifestation of antisemitism facing Australia”. 

Segal claims that anti-Israel progressives have simply repackaged an age-old hatred: 

“The language of human rights and its greatest crimes—apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc.—has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.” 

Segal doesn’t bother disputing the many well-evidenced allegations of apartheid, ethnic cleansing and genocide levelled at Israel. Nor does she consider that comparisons to the Nazis might diminish if Israel dismantled its concentration camps and Israeli politicians stopped quoting Hitler. Her report is remarkably devoid of any facts or engagement with arguments and counter-arguments. It reads like a News Corp opinion piece.

That’s because her primary objective is to dismiss criticism of Israel out of hand on the basis that it inevitably leads to anti-Jewish racism. While she concedes that criticism of Israel is not 

inherently 

antisemitic, she argues it is “utilised to create an environment where that sentiment can so easily morph into hostility towards Jewish people”. She terms this “ambient antisemitism”, which increases the danger of “conflation”, where “Jews in Australia are treated as collectively responsible for the actions of Israel”. 

There 

is

 a danger that people disgusted by Israel’s actions misdirect their anger toward Jewish people as a whole. The Palestine solidarity movement has made every effort to combat this by distinguishing between Jewish people as a politically diverse religious and ethnic group on the one hand, and the state of Israel on the other. 

Segal, for her part, reinforces this conflation. It is laid out explicitly in her report: “Jewish identity is inherently linked to the land of Israel; it is central to the existence of Jewish people, the Jewish religion and culture”. This is echoed by Israeli politicians who cynically claim to represent the 

entire Jewish community

 while committing unspeakable crimes. 

So far, these are the predictable arguments of the pro-Israel right. But as you dig deeper into the report, things get weirder. Segal thinks progressive antisemitism is dangerous not only because it legitimises criticism of Israel, but because it can act as a Trojan horse for more sinister ideologies.

Mainstream progressives are guilty, in her eyes, of “effectively laundering far-left antisemitism and Islamic extremism through a progressive lens … giving fundamentally extremist ideologies an apparently acceptable face”. 

Segal’s report makes repeated reference to this supposed intersection of radical-left politics and Islamic extremism, sanitised and promoted by respectable liberals. It is a wild conspiracy theory, one that sounds remarkably similar to Trump’s recent rants blaming rioting in France on an alliance of “migrants, jihadists, and communists”.

The language in her report mirrors that of right-wing intellectuals and government ministers overseas who rail against “Islamo-leftism”. This is the new iteration of the old myth of “Judeo-Bolshevism”, a discredited racist conspiracy theory which claimed that malign Jewish influence lay behind the Russian Revolution. This was a way for establishment reactionaries to connect their racism to their hatred of the left. 

The connecting thread is the claim that a marginalised ethnic group is engaged in a shadowy alliance with the left to undermine Western civilisation. Just as widespread antisemitism made Jews an easy target in the 1930s, Islamophobia entrenched by the so-called war on terror makes Muslims an easy target today. Muslims are painted as a fifth column, bearers of values incompatible with Australian society.

As historian Enzo Traverso noted in a 2020 

interview

 in 

Contretemps

, this “suits a xenophobic and authoritarian discourse that aims to present Islam and the radical left as objectively complicit in, if not the allies of, Islamist terrorism”. Today, as in Europe in the 1930s and France in recent years, this narrative provides justification for sweeping crackdowns on civil liberties. 

Segal’s report calls for the removal of the influence of “progressive antisemitism” from “key institutions”. She lists “universities, media, arts organisations and human rights NGOs” as areas of particular concern. In her view, mainstream media outlets have given a disproportionate and misleading view of the “conflict in the Middle East”. Universities have become hubs of pro-Palestine activism. Healthcare facilities have been riddled with “political and ideological symbols and slogans”.

Back in the real world, the mainstream media have actually 

provided cover

 for Israel’s crimes in Gaza. And the suggestion that universities have been permissive environments for the Palestine movement will come as news to many student activists who have been surveilled, suspended or threatened with expulsion by university authorities. 

Red Flag

 has 

documented

 this repression 

extensively

.

Having invented a vast problem of institutional complicity in antisemitism, Segal proposes a sweeping program to deal with it. The discredited International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which is used to delegitimise criticism of Israel, should be adopted in full across arts, sports and cultural institutions. An independent ombudsman should monitor the ABC and SBS. Social media sites should clamp down on pro-Palestine content. 

Segal’s report doesn’t just call for a further crackdown on civil liberties. She also repeats her prior calls for increased migration controls. The possibility, based on someone’s religion, cultural or national background, that they hold “antisemitic views” should be given “significant presumptive weight” when making determinations about visa applications. Generalisations about Jews and Israel are condemned, but those about people from Muslim-majority countries are actively encouraged, with visa approval dependent on “compelling countervailing considerations”.

This is further evidence that the campaign against the Palestine movement is not simply about silencing critics of Israel. It has become a vehicle for the right to pursue a much broader set of political objectives. We’ve seen a similar dynamic at the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion, where the discussion has extended to include, for instance, calls to reintroduce national service.

How could someone with such a brazenly reactionary agenda be allowed to masquerade as an anti-racism expert? The answer lies in Labor’s own role in the establishment campaign against the Palestine movement.

In appointing Jillian Segal as antisemitism envoy, Labor has created a platform for a far-right activist, cloaked in the language of “social cohesion”. Albanese has given her the opportunity to shape Australian politics, pushing an extreme pro-Israel agenda.

Labor may distance itself from the most extreme of Segal’s proposals. It has rejected an external body to monitor ABC and SBS reporting. But this should not obscure how much of her agenda has already been implemented. Already, important institutions like the healthcare worker regulator, AHPRA, have adopted the IHRA definition of antisemitism. University research grants have been denied to those accused of antisemitism. A Social Cohesion Education Hub has been set up to distribute pro-Israel material to students from pre-school to year 12. And anti-protest laws are being introduced across the country by Liberal and Labor state governments alike.

Labor has given Segal an official platform and adopted significant parts of her agenda. The result is an attack on free speech, migrants and the right to protest against genocide, under the cover of combating antisemitism and defending social cohesion.

title: Businessmen, not battlers, lead the charge for One Nation in NSW
content:
Pauline Hanson’s One Nation pretends to be a party of battlers, standing up for the little guy against the major parties. This narrative has been parroted by the mainstream media and even taken up by Hanson’s opponents. The party’s lead candidates for the March 2027 New South Wales state election paint a very different picture of who the party represents.
